record.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

record.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract Generative AI disclosure is commonly treated as a means of making manuscript production transparent. This article argues that its epistemic value is more limited. Authors may accurately report observable operations, retained outputs, and verification procedures, but functional labels such as “language polishing” or “idea generation” cannot fully reconstruct the causal contribution of AI to a finished manuscript. Nevertheless, such descriptions may strongly influence scholarly evaluation. To examine this asymmetry, the article develops the readerly distraction model, distinguishing justified provenance monitoring from disproportionate attention to features insufficiently related to the disclosed operation. Readerly distraction is analytically distinct from evaluative stigma, although disproportionate monitoring may contribute to negative perceptions of originality, competence, or trustworthiness. The model generates testable predictions concerning attention allocation, comprehension, and evaluation, including comparisons between AI assistance and functionally equivalent human mediation. The article further proposes epistemically proportionate reporting through three complementary categories: methodological reporting, governance reporting, and production-provenance disclosure. Reporting requirements should reflect the role of adopted outputs, their epistemic risks, and the procedures used to verify them rather than the quantity of AI involvement. Finally, the article develops accountable judgment as a standard of authorship comprising understanding, verification, decision authority, and answerability. Unlike nominal responsibility, accountable judgment requires capacities and procedures that can be examined when scholarly claims are challenged. Together, these proposals seek to preserve meaningful transparency without allowing speculative technological provenance to displace the evaluation of evidence and reasoning.

record.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

record.title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has altered how assessment supports learning and evidences achievement in higher education. Early institutional responses concentrated on academic integrity, detection, and task redesign, while a rapidly expanding empirical literature documents the contingent benefits and trade-offs of AI-mediated learning. This conceptual paper develops an assessment-specific framework organised around two dimensions: the distribution of learning-relevant cognitive responsibility and the visibility of student process. GenAI can operate as an engagement amplifier when it supports cognitive and metacognitive activity while preserving student responsibility for the intellectual work that matters, or as a cognitive substitute when it displaces that work while enabling successful task completion. The framework distinguishes immediate AI-supported performance from durable capability, whether demonstrated independently or with GenAI, and connects this distinction to the validity of inferences drawn from assessment evidence. Rather than proposing a universal solution to what has been called the wicked problem of AI and assessment, the framework offers an evaluative lens for judging how particular assessment configurations distribute cognitive responsibility and make student thinking visible, and whether the resulting evidence can support defensible claims about achievement. This reframing informs assessment judgements without prescribing a single model for all higher education contexts.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has challenged longstanding assumptions about the relationship between academic performance and student learning. When AI can generate essays, analyses, explanations and solutions, final products may no longer provide sufficient evidence that students engaged in the reasoning processes those products are intended to represent. This conceptual and theoretical paper proposes the IDEA framework as a thinking-centered approach to AI-enabled pedagogy. Drawing on scholarship in learning theory, reasoning, assessment and generative AI, the framework distinguishes among critical, systematic and creative thinking and connects these capacities to deductive, inductive and abductive reasoning. It further incorporates epistemic offloading and epistemic agency to examine how cognitive responsibility is distributed between learners and AI. The framework considers assignment structure, disciplinary context and learner development to determine when AI should be restricted, guided, or integrated. It also emphasizes making student reasoning, judgment, reflection and intellectual ownership visible. By shifting the focus from regulating AI use to identifying the cognitive and epistemic work that must remain meaningfully with the learner, IDEA provides a concept-to-application model for aligning generative AI with the purposes of teaching, assessment and curriculum in higher education.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Abstract The National Weather Service (NWS) recently developed an AI-powered neural machine translation system to deliver potentially life-saving weather warnings to the 68.8 million Americans who speak a language other than English at home. This forum piece makes the case that applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have a vital and largely untapped role in the continued development of this technology. First, dialect and register variation across multilingual groups demands ongoing sociolinguistic attention, as translation differences affect how people understand and conceptualize risk. Second, the metrics NWS uses to evaluate translation quality leave communicative effectiveness unmeasured, and demographic categories used to identify target audiences miss the breadth of bilingual experience, both of which applied linguistics and sociolinguistics have the tools to address. Third, indigenous, oral-tradition, and signed languages present challenges that corpus-based training cannot resolve alone, and reaching these groups will take community linguistic fieldwork and delivery beyond text. Warnings are only as effective as their comprehension, and applied linguistics can increase understanding and action during extreme weather events across a multilingual nation.

record.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines strategic content licensing between a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform and a digital news publisher in digital news markets, an important issue for understanding where AI platforms rely on publisher content while competing for user attention. It analyzes how citation intensity shapes licensing incentives, pricing, user diversion and welfare. Design/methodology/approach We develop a game-theoretic model of two-dimensional horizontal differentiation in which the AI platform has a comparative advantage in content integration and the publisher has a comparative advantage in factual accuracy. The model examines how citation intensity, hallucination risk, user preference correlation and per-use royalty jointly determine equilibrium outcomes. Findings Licensing between AI platforms and publishers arises from a trade-off between two countervailing forces: entry displacement and engagement expansion. Content licensing requires sufficiently high citation intensity; mutual gains additionally require low preference correlation. The pricing effects of citation intensity are nonmonotonic. Subscription prices can rise or fall depending on the strength of citation relative to royalty costs. User diversion is shaped by the balance between referral traffic expansion and direct substitution. Welfare improves only when engagement expansion dominates entry displacement. Originality/value This study models AI–publisher licensing in a two-dimensional Hotelling framework of asymmetric comparative advantages, conceptualizing citation intensity as a content-composition variable that shapes output quality, user traffic and royalty payments beyond existing display-level constructs.

record.title: Explainable AI for tail-risk forecasting in cryptocurrencies: evidence from green and energy-intensive assets for risk-aware investment decisions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to develop an explainable deep learning framework for forecasting tail risk and volatility in cryptocurrency markets, with a particular focus on differences between energy-intensive and ESG-oriented digital assets. It aims to assess how volatility dynamics and downside risk exposure vary across environmental profiles and market regimes and how these differences can inform risk-aware investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach The proposed framework uses a quantile long short-term memory model to estimate predictive quantiles and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), enabling the modeling of asymmetric, fat-tailed and regime-dependent risks. The analysis focuses on four cryptocurrencies – Bitcoin and Litecoin (energy-intensive) and Algorand and Chia (lower-energy alternatives). The model integrates SHapley Additive exPlanations-based explainability and a regime classification (calm vs stress). Robustness is assessed using 20-, 40- and 60-day rolling evaluation windows, while predictive performance is evaluated through coverage rates, hit ratios and Kupiec and Christoffersen back testing procedures. Findings The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across the four cryptocurrencies rather than a uniform green-versus-energy-intensive ranking. Chia records the lowest Q50 root mean squared error (0.00149) and mean absolute error (MAE) (0.00119), whereas Algorand has the lowest full-sample CVaR (0.0293) and Litecoin the highest (0.0411). Regime results are also asymmetric: Bitcoin’s Q10 violation rate rises from 8.74% in calm periods to 11.74% in stress periods, while Litecoin and Algorand record more Q10 violations in calm than in stress regimes. Chia combines the lowest global Q10 violation frequency (2.98%) with the highest mean CVaR violation loss (0.127419), showing that infrequent breaches can still be severe. These findings support asset-specific tail-risk monitoring and cautious use of energy-profile information in risk-aware investment decisions. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by integrating quantile-based deep learning, explainable artificial intelligence, regime-specific diagnostics and sustainability considerations into a unified risk-forecasting framework. Its main value lies in complementing connectedness and spillover studies with interpretable, asset-level distributional forecasts and formal tail-risk backtesting. The results provide decision-support information for risk monitoring and portfolio analysis, but do not imply that lower-energy cryptocurrencies are universally safer or that the observed differences are causal.

record.title: The AI engagement paradox: algorithmic congruence and its inverted-U effect on tourist experience quality

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
record.abstract_text: Purpose Despite widespread adoption of AI agents in restaurant and gastronomic tourism settings across Asia, practitioners consistently observe a counterintuitive pattern: increasing AI service involvement initially enhances but subsequently undermines tourist experience quality. This study aims to term this the “AI engagement paradox” and introduce algorithmic hospitality congruence (AHC), a new second-order construct to theorise and empirically confirm the inverted-U relationship between AI congruence and gastronomic tourist experience quality (GTEQ). Design/methodology/approach A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was used across three Asian markets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok). Phase 1 comprised 24 semi-structured interviews using the critical incident technique to develop AHC construct items. Phase 2 involved a quantitative survey (N = 412). AHC was grounded in cognitive load theory (CLT). Polynomial regression with response surface methodology confirmed the inverted-U effect; partial least squares structural equation modelling validated the construct. Common-method-bias mitigation and endogeneity-robustness checks used temporal separation, Harman’s single-factor test with a marker variable and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction. Findings AHC comprising culinary AI precision (CAP), emotional service resonance and cultural contextual fit (CCF) demonstrated robust construct and discriminant validity. AHC exhibited a significant inverted-U effect on GTEQ. Cultural collectivism steepened the negative slope, while digital literacy shifted the tipping point rightward. Research limitations/implications This study delivers empirically grounded deployment guidance for hospitality operators in AI-integrated gastronomic settings. The validated 15-item AHC scale provides a diagnostic instrument for monitoring AI-experience alignment. Operators are advised to benchmark their AHC composite score against the estimated tipping-point zone (4.18–5.04 on a seven-point scale), differentiate deployment intensity by tourist digital literacy, apply conservative ceiling margins for high-collectivist segments and treat CCF as a foundational design requirement rather than a localisation afterthought. Digital literacy investment is reframed as a direct hospitality revenue strategy. Originality/value This is among the first studies to theorise and empirically confirm an inverted-U effect of AI congruence in gastronomic tourism. AHC is rigorously differentiated from five related constructs and grounded in CLT from the outset. The findings challenge the linear AI benefit assumption dominant in hospitality AI research and provide indicative deployment guidance for practitioners.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: The International Journal of Information and Learning Technology
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transformed into research value within Southeast Asian universities by investigating the institutional and adaptive mechanisms linking technological capability to perceived research excellence and technology commercialization success. Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, the study develops the Institutionally Regulated Research Adaptability framework and tests it using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 2,371 respondents across 170 universities in eleven Southeast Asian countries, with institutional-level aggregation supported through within-group agreement and interclass correlation diagnostics. Findings The results demonstrate that institutional AI regulatory capacity exerts stronger effects on adaptive academic reconfiguration than foundational technological capability conditions. Dynamic research agility emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived research value realization. The proposed negative moderating effect of excessive regulatory readiness was not supported; instead, regulatory structures reinforced adaptive responsiveness. Importance–performance map analysis further identified dynamic research agility and regulatory-ethical framework readiness as the most critical strategic intervention priorities. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, while institutional aggregation may mask within-university variation. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and comparative multi-group analyses to examine national-level institutional heterogeneity across higher education systems. Practical implications Universities should prioritize institutional AI governance maturity, strengthen adaptive research agility, and strategically align faculty capability development with regulatory frameworks to translate AI capability into sustainable research and commercialization outcomes. Social implications The study highlights how institutionally coordinated AI integration can strengthen regional research ecosystems, support responsible digital transformation, and enhance Southeast Asia's academic innovation capacity within emerging knowledge economies. Originality/value This study advances AI-in-higher-education scholarship by shifting analytical focus from technology adoption to institutionally coordinated value transformation. It introduces institutionally regulated research adaptability as a novel explanatory mechanism and provides one of the first large-scale multilevel empirical examinations of GenAI-enabled research transformation across Southeast Asian higher education systems.

record.abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is to develop an understanding of AI influencer transparency and its effects on affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a conceptual synthesis of influencer marketing, consumer psychology and human–algorithm interaction research. Findings This paper introduces the Consumer–Agency Architecture (CAA) framework, distinguishing between information, control and provenance transparency. CAA posits that effects of transparency on consumer outcomes are driven by reductions in reactance, whether affective or cognitive. Information transparency primarily mitigates affective reactance; control transparency reduces cognitive reactance; and provenance transparency can attenuate both. Lower reactance, in turn, can support the formation of affective and cognitive trust, engagement and consumer well-being. The framework further identifies boundary conditions that either strengthen or weaken the relationship between transparency and reactance. Research limitations/implications This paper proposes a conceptual framework that remains to be empirically tested. It also posits that transparency effects in AI influencer marketing are primarily driven by reactance, not gains in perceived authenticity. The developed model also assumes that transparency forms have distinct rather than additive or even nonlinear effects on cognitive and affective reactance. Such assumptions could be tested in future work. Practical implications Brands and platforms should treat transparency as a portfolio of design levers rather than a single disclosure: match the specific type of transparency to the focal objective, anticipate trade-offs and avoid one-size-fits-all transparency that can erode trust. Social implications CAA provides a consumer-welfare lens for governing AI-influencer ecosystems by clarifying how transparency can support consumer agency. Originality/value CAA frames transparency in AI-influencer marketing as a means of respecting and protecting consumer agency, offering a mechanism-based foundation for designing ethically grounded, trust-sustaining AI-mediated brand relationships.

record.venue: Journal of Entrepreneurship in Emerging Economies
record.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is associated with changes in entrepreneurship education in emerging economies, focusing on entrepreneurial competencies, student cognition, venture originality and early graduate behavior. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a multisource, multicohort quasi-experimental design. Principal analyses draw on an approximately 900-student longitudinal survey and a preliminary 18-month graduate follow-up. Published evidence on educator perspectives and on 150 business plans with 45 interviews across three Chinese universities is used only for contextual triangulation and is not pooled with the study-specific statistical analyses. Findings In the principal student analyses, generative AI was associated with stronger opportunity recognition but lower divergent thinking and higher confirmation bias. Predictive analytics was associated with more evidence-based evaluation, while structured intelligent tutoring was associated with stronger metacognitive reflection. Published business-plan evidence is used only to contextualize homogenization. The 18-month venture-creation differences were not statistically significant and remain exploratory. Research limitations/implications The nonrandomized design, incomplete wave-specific attrition information, unavailable matching diagnostics, reliance on published contextual evidence for homogenization and educator perspectives and short follow-up period limit causal claims and cross-context generalization. Future studies should use controlled designs, complete longitudinal reporting, longer graduate tracking and cross-country comparisons. record.abstract_text: The contemporary literary landscape has been fundamentally reshaped by the rise of Instapoetry: short, visual, and emotionally direct verse disseminated primarily through Instagram, a platform whose image-first architecture and recommender systems privilege affectively engaging content. This article argues that the dominance of this poetic form represents not a superficial cultural trend but an adaptive response to a digitally mediated attention economy. It advances an integrative theoretical framework explaining Instapoetry through the convergence of three dimensions: algorithmic, psychological, and cultural. First, algorithmic amplification on Instagram leverages patterns of repetition and social proof to promote specific formal styles. Second, the cognitive state of the platform’s users—marked by social media fatigue and elevated cognitive load—produces a preference for content high in processing fluency. Third, the cultural motifs that dominate Instapoetry function as accessible affective schemas, enabling readers to engage in self-expression, identity construction, and emotional validation. Drawing on research in media studies, cognitive science, and feminist literary criticism—and referencing the influential work of early Instapoets such as Rupi Kaur and Amanda Lovelace—this paper proposes a multidisciplinary account of how digital infrastructures and human psychology jointly shape contemporary poetic production and reception.

This provides empirical evidence for the reform of emergency medicine education and emphasizes the importance of linking educational process evaluation with clinical outcomes.

The threat comes from humans who use AI to appropriate its output and extract the value attached to human effort. This process is compounded by the difficulty of verifying declared human authorship or inventorship, which may reward deception and discourage honest effort. I therefore explore value migration from execution skill to concentrated complementary assets. Findings: Research has shifted from technology acceptance toward ethics and governance, although it remains dominated by higher education and cross-sectional designs. Responsible AI principles include transparency, accountability, fairness, and human oversight. The Islamic perspective strengthens these principles through maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah and the values of amanah, 'adl, ihsan, sidq, and tabayyun. The relationship between AI and human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity is conditional: reflective and verified use tends to support these dimensions, whereas dependence may undermine them. Novelty: This review's findings point to a shift from governance-centered responsibility to moral-epistemic responsibility, with three propositions: tabayyun as an obligation of epistemic verification, hifẓ al-‘aql as an educational orientation, and integrating AI governance with moral-educational development. Contribution: This study provides a conceptual foundation for responsible AI use in Islamic education by placing human oversight, information verification, independent thinking, and academic integrity at its core. Future Research: Future studies should test these propositions through longitudinal and experimental designs and develop instruments that integrate Islamic ethical values, human agency, cognitive autonomy, and academic integrity. record.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology
record.abstract_text: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become useful tools for analysing medical images because they can learn visual patterns associated with normal and abnormal tissue. In cancer screening and diagnosis, however, a high classification score alone is not sufficient: clinicians also need to understand which image regions influenced a model’s output. This paper proposes an explainable deep-learning framework that combines CNN-based image classification with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to support early cancer detection from histopathological images. The proposed workflow includes image collection, quality assessment, preprocessing, augmentation, CNN training, prediction, and explanation generation. Grad-CAM is used to produce class-specific heatmaps, while LIME and SHAP are considered for local image-region and feature-contribution explanations. The explanations are intended to help users inspect whether the model focuses on tissue regions that are relevant to the predicted class rather than irrelevant background patterns. Model performance can be assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and area under the ROC curve. Explanation quality should additionally be examined through localization agreement, stability, and review by qualified domain experts. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its diagnostic performance and clinical usefulness must be established through controlled experiments and external validation. It is designed as a decision-support approach and is not intended to replace professional diagnosis.

record.abstract_text: Consumers can use sustainability information to consume responsibly; however, excessive and complex sustainability claims might confuse consumers and hinder proper evaluations. GAIL significantly moderated the SIO-GIVB relationship: SIO was negatively associated with GIVB at low GAIL but not significantly at mean or high GAIL.GIVB positively influenced GPDC. An indirect effect of SIO on GPDC through GIA is significant, but the indirect effect through GIVB is not significant unconditionally. From a practical perspective, sustainability portals and shopping applications involving GenAI should emphasize evaluability and verifiability rather than enhancing disclosures. record.abstract_text: University students, particularly those who also work or hold organizational roles, frequently experience academic overload, stress, and burnout. Existing digital tools tend to address either task management or well-being, rarely both, and many lose users within days. This study reports the evidence-informed design of StudyFlow, a mobile-first platform that helps students turn unstructured academic demands into a prioritized, actionable plan, and examines how its design aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A design science research approach was followed. A targeted narrative review of literature published from 2021 to 2026 on student stress, working students, digital well-being interventions, engagement, and gamification informed a proto-persona, eight use cases, and nine functional requirements. A high-fidelity interactive prototype was generated through a five-stage natural-language prompt sequence in Google Stitch and refined in Google AI Studio. The intended feature set was compared with four widely used productivity and well-being applications, and each feature group was mapped to SDG targets with measurable evaluation indicators. The review yielded seven design implications, each traced to specific requirements and interface decisions. The prototype implements a four-stage workflow (set up, capture, organize and act, reflect) across dashboard, brain dump, task, focus, insights, and settings screens. None of the four comparator applications supported academic assignment breakdown, and none combined task capture, prioritization, focus support, reflection, and progress feedback in a single workflow. Streaks and usage metrics were deliberately framed as optional, non-punitive cues. StudyFlow shows how evidence on student stress and app engagement can be translated into a coherent, low-friction design that targets student well-being (SDG Target 3.4), persistence in tertiary education (Target 4.3), and the inclusion of working students (Target 10.2). Because no user testing has yet been conducted, no effectiveness claims are made; a staged usability and pilot evaluation protocol is proposed.

record.abstract_text: This study investigates how generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and business analytics capability shape strategic financial decision quality in emerging market SMEs, with particular attention to the moderating role of AI governance maturity. Grounded in organizational information processing theory and dynamic capabilities theory, the study argues that better financial decisions depend not simply on access to advanced technologies, but on how effectively firms turn AI generated forecasts and analytical information into useful financial judgment. AI governance maturity is expected to strengthen this process by providing appropriate oversight, accountability, validation, and control over the use of AI generated financial information. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 385 respondents who possessed relevant knowledge of SME financial management, business analytics, AI applications, or organizational decision making. Data were collected using a five-point Likert scale questionnaire and analyzed with IBM SPSS version 26. Reliability analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and multiple linear regression were performed, while Hayes’ Process Macro Model 1 was used to test the moderating effect. The results show that generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability (β = 0.613) and business analytics capability (β = 0.487) both have significant positive effects on strategic financial decision quality. AI governance maturity also strengthens the relationship between generative AI enabled financial forecasting capability and strategic financial decision quality, with an interaction coefficient of 0.518. These findings suggest that emerging market SMEs gain greater value from generative AI when forecasting tools are supported by sound analytical capabilities and governance practices. Effective financial decision making therefore requires not only better technology, but also the organizational capacity to interpret, review, and responsibly use AI generated financial insights.

record.abstract_text: In a global information environment characterised by strong propaganda pressures and a lack of transparency, the demand for independent, high-quality sources is constantly growing. A significant gap is thus emerging between the growing complexity of information flows and users' ability to critically evaluate information. Currently, neither information professionals nor engaged citizens are able to accurately verify every single piece of news, nor do they have access to online platforms capable of selecting, verifying, and aggregating thematic content based on shared quality criteria. The lack of human and technical resources severely hinders the creation of information ecosystems resilient to disinformation. To address this challenge, recent efforts have focused on integrated platforms that combine human expertise with advanced automated analysis tools. Technologies such as machine learning, semantic analysis, and generative artificial intelligence offer innovative solutions for processing large volumes of data and supporting automated fact-checking. Nonetheless, the evolution of these technologies introduces new complexities, reshaping content production and distribution. Algorithms often amplify information polarisation. Traditional media increasingly align with partisan political and economic interests, losing credibility. As a result, citizens align themselves with different news sources in an attempt to reconstruct the truth within a fragmented digital landscape. By bringing together the analysis of manipulative strategies, the evolution of verification methods, hybrid human–AI workflows, and the requirements of explainability within a single survey, the article aims to offer researchers and practitioners a more integrated reference point for the design of effective and accountable verification systems.

record.abstract_text: This qualitative case study examined how ten secondary school ESL students in Malaysia used ChatGPT when revising their writing. The study did not focus on writing scores. Instead, it looked at students’ writing behaviours, the decisions they made when using ChatGPT, and the changes that appeared between their first and revised drafts. The students first wrote an essay on “Having a Balanced Diet” without using ChatGPT. After a short introduction to the tool, students revised the same essay with the help of ChatGPT. Data collection took place through writing samples from the students and semi-structured interviews. The interview data were analysed using thematic analysis, while the comparison between the first and the second drafts was conducted using document analysis. From the findings, it is clear that the students made use of ChatGPT to go through grammar, vocabulary, sentence structure, and content of their essays. Many improvements had been made in the revised drafts. Most of the students managed to fix grammar errors and use more suitable vocabulary, along with presenting new ideas in their work. Nonetheless, there are some flaws in the second drafts such as incorrect expressions, informal language and some incorrect ideas. The interviews also showed that the students did not accept the suggestions directly. The students chose those suggestions which were clear to them, appropriate to the task and related to their original meaning. Overall, the study shows that ChatGPT may be used to support ESL writing revision but students still need teacher guidance and their own judgement to use it critically and responsibly.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

record.venue: Journal of Education, Humanities and Social Sciences
record.abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence now belongs to ordinary adolescent life, but the psychological research that should guide its design spreads over fields which seldom cite each other. Research on adolescent development, on misinformation susceptibility, on trust in automation, on chatbot-supported learning and on companion-chatbot overreliance has grown up separately, and each of these areas answers only part of the question of how a general-purpose chatbot should talk to a teenager. This paper brings together twenty-one sources from developmental psychology, human factors, human-computer interaction and educational technology, in order to show what is now known about adolescent chatbot interaction and what this means for conversational design. Three results appear repeatedly in this research. First, adolescence is a design context of its own, not a smaller version of adulthood, since reward sensitivity, social influence and emotional regulation are still developing, while exposure to persuasive conversational systems has already reached almost everyone. Second, trust in a chatbot changes behavior in ways that can be measured; thus, the proper design target is calibrated trust rather than maximal trust. Third, the failure modes that matter most for adolescent users, that is, hallucination, sycophancy and unwarranted confidence, originate in the model; the user is not their source. From these results this paper consolidates ten conversational design principles into four clusters, namely epistemic calibration, metacognitive scaffolding, bounded emotional support and autonomy preservation. The framework here is a conceptual synthesis and puts forward testable predictions, but it has not been empirically validated.

record.abstract_text: The increasing use of automation and advanced machinery in modern industries has made equipment reliability and operational efficiency important factors in industrial production. Unexpected machine failures can interrupt production activities, increase maintenance expenses, and affect overall productivity. Traditional maintenance approaches, such as reactive and preventive maintenance, are often unable to identify early signs of equipment failure or accurately determine when maintenance is actually required. To overcome these limitations, this paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Digital Twin technology for predictive maintenance in industrial environments. A Digital Twin is a virtual representation of a physical machine or industrial system that is continuously updated using data collected from sensors installed on the actual equipment. By combining this technology with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning algorithms, it becomes possible to monitor equipment conditions, analyse operational patterns, detect abnormal behaviour, and predict potential failures before they cause major interruptions. The proposed approach integrates Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, real-time data acquisition, data preprocessing, virtual equipment modelling, and AI-based predictive analysis into a unified maintenance framework. Machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks can be applied for fault detection, condition monitoring, and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation. This paper presents a case-study-based investigation of AI-enabled Digital Twins for industrial equipment monitoring, with particular emphasis on understanding how real-time data and predictive analytics can improve maintenance planning. It also examines the system architecture, working methodology, potential advantages, implementation challenges, and limitations of the proposed approach. The study highlights the potential of integrating AI with Digital Twin technology to transform conventional maintenance practices into more intelligent, data-driven, and condition-based systems, thereby supporting improved equipment reliability, reduced unplanned downtime, and more efficient industrial operations. record.venue: International Journal of Business and Management (IJBM)
record.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping organizational work, yet its behavioural consequences for employees remain unevenly understood. Existing research on productivity, creativity and engagement is fragmented and rarely examined within a single theoretical framework. Drawing on Job Demands Resources theory, Conservation of Resources theory and Self Determination Theory, this conceptual paper develops an integrative model of how organizational GenAI adoption affects employee productivity, creativity and work engagement. Job crafting is proposed as the central behavioural mechanism. The model treats GenAI as both a job resource and a job demand. It therefore recognizes a double edged pathway in which technology insecurity and passive over reliance can offset the benefits of adoption. AI literacy, ethical use clarity and organizational readiness are identified as boundary conditions that determine which pathway prevails. Four hypotheses are developed, covering the mediating role of job crafting for productivity and engagement, its moderating role for creativity, and the conditioning effect of AI literacy and ethical guidance. A time lagged, multi source survey design, supplemented by supervisor ratings and an optional field experiment, is proposed for future empirical testing. The paper offers a resource based account of human and AI collaboration. Practically, organizations should complement investments in AI capabilities with transparent, explainable, and fair AI governance and engagement-oriented work design to preserve and develop human resources during digital transformation. Longitudinal and cross-national research is therefore needed to examine whether these relationships persist over time and contribute to long-term employee and organizational resilience.
